power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Peers are hypothesized to influence adolescent mental health.
However, most peer effects studies are susceptible to selection bias and reverse causation, limiting causal inference.
Objective Examine classroom peer effects using a genetically informed approach and quasi-random classroom assignment.

Nationwide primary and specialist care registry data were used to follow a cohort of 750 750 Norwegian adolescents born between 1998 and 2010 until first registered psychiatric diagnosis, emigration, death, or December 31 2023.
School class, school, and residential area at age 13 were identified.
Data were analyzed from March to October 2026.
Exposures (1) Pearson-Aitken Family-Genetic Risk Scores (FGRSs) indexing genetic liability to psychiatric disorders for individuals and peers sharing classroom, school, and/or residential area.
Classrooms did not differ systematically in FGRSs, demonstrating that classroom peer FGRSs served as a natural experiment of quasi-randomization into peer environments.
(2) Peers' psychiatric diagnoses.
Registrations for alcohol use disorder (AUD), drug use disorder (DUD), major depression (MD), and anxiety diagnoses.
Associations with classroom peer FGRSs and interaction effects with individual genetic liability and sex were estimated using discrete-time survival and Cox proportional hazards models.
Psychiatric disorder risk was partly clustered at the classroom level (proportions of explained variance 0.9-5.0%).
One SD increase in classroom risk was associated with a hazard ratio [HR] of 1.26 for AUD, 1.53 for DUD, and 1.18 for MD, and 1.20 for anxiety disorders.

Classroom peer FGRSs were associated with increased risk of AUD in early adolescence (highest vs. lowest peer FGRS quintile, HR: 1.18; 95% CI 1.04, 1.34), MD (HR: 1.10; 95% CI, 1.06-1.14), and anxiety (HR, 1.07; 95% CI, 1.03-1.11).
Classmate diagnoses were associated with elevated risk of DUD, MD, and anxiety (HRs: 1.02-1.16).
No interaction effects between classroom peer FGRSs and genetic liability were observed; classroom peer FGRSs estimated for females predicted a higher risk among females (interaction HRs: 1.02-1.04).
We found evidence of classroom peer effects, unbiased by selection bias and reverse causation, on internalizing disorder and AUD risk in early adolescence.
Future studies are necessary to understand traits and mechanisms involved.

Adolescence is characterized by elevated risk of mental health problems. 1 Many diagnoses have their peak age of onset around 14 years 2 and the prevalence of mental disorders increases across childhood to 14% between ages 16 and 19. 3 Strong links are observed between adolescent mental health and later health outcomes, indicating that the foundations for mental health in adulthood are partially established in this period. 4 Peer interactions represent a long hypothesized influence on adolescent mental health, 5, 6 a notion supported by several lines of empirical research.

Two recent studies examined peer effects using genetic liability estimates of school peers to find that peer family-genetic risk scores (FGRSs) predict elevated risk of psychiatric disorders. 15, 16 A strength of this approach is virtually eliminating the risk of reverse confounding: FGRSs are calculated for each person based on the diagnostic history of family members and are unaffected by peer behaviors.

text.text: As such, this design mirrors genomic designs quantifying environmentally mediated genetic effects on mental health. [17] [18] [19] However, genetically informed peer effects studies remain susceptible to the potential impact of selection bias, i.e., if students at elevated risk cluster systematically in certain social environments. 15 Several questions pertaining to peer effects on psychiatric disorders are unexplored.

text.text: First, no genetically informed studies have examined classroom-level peer effects.

The classroom is a hub for friendship networks in school and an important context for social interactions. 20, 21 Delineating peer effects at the classroom level could have implications for identifying mechanisms involved and potential targets for intervention.

text.text: Furthermore, Norwegian law mandates that classroom allocation occurs generally independent of individual characteristics. 22 As such, peer FGRSs indexing the genetic liability of classmates could be leveraged as quasi-random exposures minimizing selection bias and strengthening casual inference.

text.text: Second, sex-specific patterns in psychiatric disorder burden in adolescents 3 raise the possibility that etiological influences, including peer effects, differ across females and males.

text.text: Few studies have examined such differences.

Here, we examine peer effects on risk of alcohol use disorder (AUD), drug use disorder (DUD), major depression (MD), and anxiety disorders using nationwide health, educational, and residential registry data for all adolescents born between 1998 and 2010 in Norway.

We apply a genetically informed approach to answer four research questions: (i) Is psychiatric disorder risk clustered in classrooms, i.e., are individuals in the same class more similar in subsequent psychiatric disorder risk?
; (ii) do classmate diagnoses and classroom peer FGRSs predict psychiatric disorder risk independent of individual genetic liability?
; (iii) do classroom peer FGRSs interact with individual genetic liability in predicting psychiatric disorder risk?
; (iv) do classroom peer FGRSs interact with sex in predicting psychiatric disorder risk?

Finally, we examined associations between classroom FGRSs and birth length as a negative control analysis, 23 expecting peer FGRSs associated with psychiatric disorder risk to be unrelated to birth length.
text.formatted: Finally, we examined associations between classroom FGRSs and birth length as a negative control analysis, <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">23</ref> expecting peer FGRSs associated with psychiatric disorder risk to be unrelated to birth length.

text.text: This study was based on pseudonymized data from population registries in Norway, which do not require personal informed consent, and approved by the Regional Committees for Medical and Health Research Ethics (2017/2205).

We describe the sample, analyses, and results in accordance with the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) guidelines. 24 Our population included all residents in Norway born between 1998 and 2010 who had not died or permanently emigrated prior to 2010 (N = 931 582).
text.formatted: We describe the sample, analyses, and results in accordance with the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) guidelines. <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">24</ref> Our population included all residents in Norway born between 1998 and 2010 who had not died or permanently emigrated prior to 2010 (N = 931 582).

text.text: We further restricted the analytic sample to participants with available information on classrooms, schools, and residential areas at age 13 (N = 750 750).
We identified registrations with primary and specialist healthcare services for any diagnosis of interest from January 1, 2011, through December 31, 2023.
Participants were observed from age 13 until emigration, death, or December 31 st , 2023, whichever came first.
Primary healthcare data were incorporated from the Norwegian Control and Payment of Health Reimbursements Database (KUHR), available from 2006 to 2023.
Specialist healthcare data were incorporated from the Norwegian Patient Register (NPR), available from 2008 to 2023.

We identified registrations for diagnoses in accordance with the International Classification of Primary Care, Second Revision (ICPC-2) for KUHR and the International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems, Tenth Revision (ICD-10) for NPR.
We included diagnoses of AUD, DUD, MD, and anxiety disorders (an overview is provided in Tables 2 and S1).
text.formatted: We included diagnoses of AUD, DUD, MD, and anxiety disorders (an overview is provided in Tables <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">2</ref> and <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">S1</ref>).

text.text: For each participant, we included indicators for classroom, school cohort, and residential area cohort at 13 years of age.

Classrooms were identified based on national test data completed in 8 th grade of lower secondary school from 2011 to 2023. 25 As noted, it is mandated by Norwegian law that allocation to classrooms occurs in general independent of individual characteristics such as ethnicity, gender, and academic level. 22, 26 The mean class size in eight grade in Norway is 22 students (standard deviation, SD, 9). 27 We therefore excluded classroom indicators with fewer than 10 or more than 35 students.

text.text: We created school cohort indicators by combining school identification number with the year of test completion to identify individuals who were students in the same school at the same time.
Finally, we created residential area cohort indicators by combining information on county and subarea 28 with birth year to identify individuals who were of similar ages in the same residential area.

text.text: We excluded residential area indicators with at least 5 individuals to reduce the impact of areas with limited information (i.e., very small peer groups).
We calculated Pearson-Aitken FGRSs following the approach of Krebs et al. 29 for AUD, DUD, MD, and anxiety disorders.

text.text: The Pearson-Aitken FGRS is based on a liability-threshold model. 30 For each individual, we used a population graph of parent-offspring linkages and diagnostic history of family members to update the posterior expectation of each index person's additive genetic liability.

text.text: Prior liability ranges were constructed based on diagnostic status and cumulative incidence proportions specific to participants' sex and ages-at-risk to account for left-truncation and censoring.

FGRS estimation was conducted using LTFGRS. 31 Further details of Pearson-Aitken FGRSs implemented in Norwegian registries are reported in Bjørndal et al. 32 For each indicator (classroom, school cohort, residential area cohort), we computed a corresponding peer mean FGRS excluding the focal individual, to ensure that one's own FGRS did not contribute to the peer FGRS.

text.text: Quasi-random allocation to classrooms should result in classes being uncorrelated in familial liability to psychiatric disorders conditional on schools and residential areas (i.e., accounting for schools and residential areas, there should be little selection of students by risk into different classrooms).

We examined systematic differences in FGRSs between classrooms using a multilevel linear regression model with each FGRS as the outcome and random intercepts for classrooms, school cohort, and residential area cohort.
We computed the intraclass correlation (ICC) as the proportion of variance explained at the classroom level.

All models adjusted for sex and sociodemographic variables at age 13 (i.e., parental income, unemployment, and education) and were estimated using lme4. 34 FGRSs were not substantially clustered at the classroom level with ICC estimates ranging from 0.1-0.3% (Tables S2 and S3).

text.text: We investigated peer effects on psychiatric disorder risk using a genetically informed approach, quasi-random classroom allocation, and nationwide registry data for Norwegian adolescents.
We describe three key findings.
First, adolescents sharing the same classrooms in early adolescence were more similar in subsequent psychiatric disorder risk, in particular for AUD and DUD.
Second, classroom peer FGRSs were associated with risk of AUD (in early adolescence only), MD, and anxiety disorders.

Third, we found limited evidence of interaction effects between classroom peer FGRSs and individual genetic liability or sex, although peer FGRSs for females were more strongly associated with diagnosis risk among females.

We provide evidence of peer effects originating in school classes using a genetically informed approach and extending previous work using school and residential indicators to identify peers 15, 16 : being in a class with a higher average peer FGRS composition was associated with an increase in AUD and internalizing disorder risk.

text.text: No peer FGRS association was observed for DUD which might be explained by its lower prevalence and less powerful FGRS.
On the contrary, having classmate diagnosed with DUD in early adolescence predicted subsequent risk.
The relevance of the school class context for adolescent mental health is also evident in the excess similarity among students sharing classrooms in subsequent psychiatric disorder risk.

This quantification of clustering across contexts aligns with a socio-ecological perspective on development. 6 We provide the first investigation of classroom peer effects integrating peer FGRSs and quasirandom class allocation to strengthen causal inference.

text.text: To this end, our study can be compared to previous natural experiments applied in peer effects research.

For instance, studies have leveraged random roommate allocation in college and found peer effects on both binge drinking 40 and selfreported mental health outcomes. 41 Our study design addresses two common limitations in the peer effects literature 11 : reliance on perceptions of peer behaviors (by indexing peer effects with peer FGRSs) and absence of experimental evidence (by leveraging quasi-random allocation to classrooms).

text.text: Our findings are agnostic to specific traits and mechanisms involved in classroom peer effects.
These might include higher mental health awareness and more frequent help-seeking behaviors in some peer networks originating in classes.

Qualitative studies have highlighted the important roles of peers and school personnel in encouraging help-seeking for adolescents with mental health difficulties. 42 More positive teacher-student relationships are broadly associated with better emotional and behavioral outcomes in students 43 and may offer a protective mechanism.

text.text: School classrooms provide an important context for establishing friendships and social relationships. 20 Theoretical frameworks for peer effects emphasize the importance of social learning behaviors, the affirmation of identity, and needs for belonging. 11 Delineating the specific processes involved, which may also differ across diagnoses, is an important aim for future studies.

text.text: Strengths of our study include the integration of nationwide health, educational and residential registry data for all Norwegian adolescents born between 1998 and 2010 and a robust study design minimizing reverse confounding and selection bias.
However, our findings should be interpreted in the context of some important limitations.

First, although Norwegian law mandates that classroom allocation should occur generally unrelated to individual characteristics and our analyses indicated that classrooms did not differ systematically in familial liability, our study design was not fully randomized.
Thus, we cannot be certain that observed associations between peer FGRSs and diagnosis risk are not impacted by unmeasured confounding.
Second, the ICC for binary outcomes may be overestimated when prevalence is low. 44 Thus, uncertainty remains regarding the magnitude of clustering of psychiatric disorder risk.
text.formatted: Second, the ICC for binary outcomes may be overestimated when prevalence is low. <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">44</ref> Thus, uncertainty remains regarding the magnitude of clustering of psychiatric disorder risk.

text.text: Third, we could not assess peer effects on less severe mental health outcomes and were restricted to identify classrooms at age 13 years as classroom indicator data were available for secondary school only.
However, most students would be expected to share the same classroom until approximately 16 years (end of secondary school).
Fourth, our findings are limited to a Norwegian context and their generalizability is unclear

Our findings provide evidence for classmate peer effects, unbiased by selection bias and reverse causation, on internalizing disorder and AUD risk using a genetically informed approach and quasi-random allocation of students to classrooms.
This suggests that peer effects represent one etiological factor in psychiatric disorder risk in adolescence and young adulthood.
